mean: make something clear by giving details or reasons
ex: Mrs Rao asked the lineman to explain why her electricity bill had doubled in May.
note: Say 'explain it to me', never 'explain me'. This is one of the most common Indian English errors.
ex2: Can you explain the rules of kabaddi to my friend from Germany before the match starts?

mean: put forward an idea or plan for others to think about
ex: Can I suggest we leave for Lonavala at five, before the expressway traffic builds up?
note: Say 'suggest that we go' or 'suggest going', not 'suggest us to go'.
ex2: What would you suggest for a first trip to Kerala during the monsoon?

mean: say that you are unhappy or annoyed about something
ex: Residents of Sector 12 decided to complain to the municipal office about the overflowing drains.
note: Complain ABOUT a thing, TO a person. 'Crib' (complain) is informal; use 'complain' in formal writing.
ex2: Passengers on the delayed Rajdhani began to complain when the pantry ran out of tea.

mean: tell someone about a danger or problem before it happens
ex: The weather office sent alerts to warn fishermen in Odisha not to go to sea for three days.
note: Warn someone OF or ABOUT a danger, or warn them NOT TO do something. Noun: warning.
ex2: Grandma always tries to warn us not to swim in the village pond after dark.

mean: speak or write about something briefly
ex: Did Farhan mention that the parent-teacher meeting has been moved to Saturday?
note: You mention a thing, not 'mention about' it. 'Not to mention' adds a bigger point: 'tiring, not to mention costly'.
ex2: Please mention your roll number on every page of the answer sheet.

mean: say firmly that something must happen or is true, and not back down
ex: Nani will always insist that we eat something before leaving, even if we just had lunch.
note: 'Insist on doing', not 'insist to do'. In Indian homes, a host who insists is being hospitable, not rude.
ex2: If the shopkeeper says the price is fixed, don't insist on a discount; just walk to the next stall.

mean: make something clearer by explaining it more
ex: The college put up a notice to clarify that the exams would be held offline, not online.
note: Clarify removes confusion that already exists; explain can start from zero.
ex2: Could you clarify whether the wedding dinner is pure veg? My uncle eats no onion or garlic either.

mean: give special importance to a point by stressing it
ex: The doctor wanted to emphasise one thing: finish the full course of antibiotics, even if you feel better.
note: 'Emphasise the point', not 'emphasise ON the point'. Only the noun takes 'on': 'emphasis on'. US spelling: emphasize.
ex2: Before every raid, the kabaddi coach would emphasise one thing: hold your breath and stay low.

mean: say something briefly as a comment or opinion
ex: It is rude to remark on someone's weight at a family wedding, however close the aunty is.
note: Also a noun. A 'passing remark' is a quick, unplanned comment. Remark on/about something.
ex2: Did you hear the commentator remark that the pitch looked like a Chennai road in May?

mean: tell someone firmly that something is true, to remove their doubt
ex: I can assure you, sir, the parcel will reach Guwahati by Monday.
note: You assure a PERSON; you ensure something happens; you insure against loss. Three different words.
ex2: The tailor tried to assure Fatima that her blouse would be ready well before the sangeet.

mean: say something indirectly and let others guess what you mean
ex: Pooja tried to hint that she wanted a book, not jewellery, for her birthday this year.
note: Also a noun. 'Drop a hint' is the common phrase; a 'broad hint' is a very obvious one.
ex2: My cousin dropped such a big hint about the surprise party that we all knew by Sunday.

mean: strongly advise or ask someone to do something
ex: Doctors urge everyone to drink boiled or filtered water during the monsoon.
note: Stronger than 'advise', politer than 'order'. As a noun it means a sudden strong wish: 'an urge to eat samosas'.
ex2: Teachers urge students not to copy answers from the internet for their science projects.

mean: say something to make a worried person feel calmer
ex: The pilot came on the speaker to reassure passengers that the bumpy ride over the Western Ghats was normal.
note: Assure = tell firmly that something is true; reassure = remove worry, often again and again. Reassure is about feelings.
ex2: Before the operation, the nurse held Dadi's hand to reassure her that everything would be fine.

mean: reply quickly and sharply, often with anger or wit
ex: When the anchor kept interrupting, the panellist was quick to retort, 'Please let me finish one sentence.'
note: A retort is a sharp comeback; a reply is any answer. It is also a noun: 'a sharp retort'.
ex2: When his sister called him lazy, Kunal was quick to retort that at least he made his own chai.

mean: speak quietly and unclearly, usually because you are annoyed
ex: Stuck at Silk Board junction, the auto driver began to mutter about the endless metro work.
note: Mutter usually carries a complaint; mumble is just unclear speech; whisper is quiet on purpose.
ex2: On the crowded bus, Rinku heard an old man mutter something about young people and their phones.

mean: suggest something without saying it directly
ex: Are you trying to imply that I ate the last laddoo?
note: The speaker implies; the listener infers. 'Are you implying I'm late?' is right; 'Are you inferring...?' is a common mix-up.
ex2: The headline seemed to imply the bridge was unsafe, but the report said only the paint was peeling.

mean: give more details about something you have said
ex: The interviewer asked Ritu to elaborate on her role in the hackathon project.
note: The verb ends '-rayt'; the adjective ('an elaborate wedding') ends '-rut'. Say 'elaborate on', not 'elaborate about'.
ex2: The bride's mother refused to elaborate on the menu, saying only that it would be a surprise.

mean: admit that something is true, or publicly thank someone for their work
ex: At the farewell, the principal paused to acknowledge the support staff who had kept the school running.
note: 'Please acknowledge receipt' is office English for 'tell me you got it'. The silent k: say uk-NOL-ij.
ex2: The captain was big enough to acknowledge that the other side had simply played better.

mean: express your thoughts or feelings clearly in words
ex: Many students know the answer but struggle to articulate it during a viva.
note: As an adjective ('an articulate speaker') it ends '-lut' and means able to express ideas clearly.
ex2: At the district meeting, the young farmer was able to articulate the village's water problem clearly.

mean: mention something indirectly, without naming it
ex: In his wedding speech, Vikram seemed to allude to the groom's many failed driving tests.
note: Always 'allude to'. Don't confuse it with 'elude' (escape). Allude is an indirect mention; 'refer to' can be direct.
ex2: The title of the new film seems to allude to an old Raj Kapoor song.

mean: say something again to make it clear or stress it
ex: The coach wanted to reiterate that nobody skips fielding practice before the Ranji match.
note: Don't write 'reiterate again': the 're' already means again. A favourite word of press statements.
ex2: The cabin crew had to reiterate that phones must be switched off, as many passengers ignored the first announcement.

mean: move away from the main topic while speaking or writing
ex: Our history professor would often digress into long stories about his village near Darbhanga.
note: 'But I digress' is a polite way to say 'back to the point'. Noun: digression.
ex2: Let me digress for a moment and tell you how my grandparents first met at a village mela.

mean: short and clear, with no extra words
ex: Keep the WhatsApp update concise: time, venue and what to bring for the picnic.
note: Concise means short AND complete; brief means only short. Noun: conciseness. Cutting extra words makes writing concise.
ex2: Anjali's concise answer in the board exam scored full marks, while longer answers lost points.

mean: speaking or writing in a beautiful, powerful and moving way
ex: The retired judge gave an eloquent farewell speech that left the whole courtroom in tears.
note: Eloquent moves people; articulate is simply clear. An 'eloquent silence' says a lot without words.
ex2: The young lawyer's eloquent argument in the Allahabad High Court impressed even the opposing side.

mean: using very few words, sometimes in a dry or cool way
ex: Asked how the Himalayan trek went, my laconic cousin from Shimla just said, 'Cold. Good.'
note: Laconic usually describes a person or way of speaking; concise describes a piece of writing. Named after the famously brief Spartans of Laconia.
ex2: The laconic old farmer answered every question about the drought with a single nod.

mean: a soft or polite word used instead of a harsh or awkward one
ex: At the Bengaluru startup, 'restructuring' turned out to be a euphemism for firing forty people.
note: 'Passed away' for died, 'let go' for fired. Not a lie, but it can hide a hard truth; good writers notice them.
ex2: In many families, 'not keeping well' is a euphemism for an illness nobody wants to name.

mean: say what someone or something is like
ex: Can you describe the man who snatched your bag at Dadar station?
note: Describe something, not 'describe about something'.
ex2: Grandpa loves to describe the Lucknow of his childhood, with tongas and kites on every roof.

mean: answer someone who has spoken or written to you
ex: Please reply to the wedding card by Friday so the caterer knows how many plates to plan.
note: Reply TO someone: 'please reply to me', not 'please reply me'.
ex2: When the teacher asked who broke the window, nobody in the class dared to reply.

mean: tell many people something officially, often for the first time
ex: The station master will announce the platform for the Howrah Mail ten minutes before it arrives.
note: You announce news to a group; you tell one person.
ex2: At the family dinner, Sneha stood up to announce that she had got into medical college.

mean: stop someone while they are speaking
ex: Please don't interrupt Dadi while she is telling her story; let her finish.
note: 'Sorry to interrupt, but...' is the polite way to cut in at a meeting.
ex2: In the news debate, the anchor would interrupt every guest before they made a single point.

mean: make something sound bigger, better or worse than it is
ex: Fishermen in our village always exaggerate the size of the fish that got away.
note: Spelt with double g and one r: exaggerate.
ex2: Don't exaggerate; the queue at the passport office was long, but it was not five kilometres.

mean: say that someone or something is good and worth choosing
ex: Can you recommend a good dhaba on the highway between Delhi and Jaipur?
note: 'I recommend that you try it' or 'I recommend trying it' sounds better than 'recommend you to try'.
ex2: My professor agreed to recommend me for the summer internship at a Bengaluru research lab.

mean: admit something wrong or embarrassing that you did
ex: Rahul had to confess that he had broken the TV remote while playing cricket indoors.
note: 'I must confess...' is a soft way to make a small, honest admission.
ex2: I must confess I have never watched a single episode of the serial my whole family loves.

mean: make an idea or feeling known to someone
ex: Please convey my good wishes to your parents on their silver anniversary.
note: 'Please convey my regards' is a polite formula common in Indian letters and emails.
ex2: A good teacher can convey the beauty of a Tagore poem even to a restless Class 9.

mean: give only the main points, briefly
ex: At the end of the meeting, Deepa will summarise what each team must finish by Monday.
note: British and Indian spelling: summarise. American: summarize.
ex2: Can you summarise the last episode for me? I missed it because of the power cut.

mean: talk for a long time in a confused way, without a clear point
ex: Nervous in his first interview, Sameer began to ramble about his school cricket team instead of the job.
note: 'Ramble on' is common. A ramble is also a long, easy walk in the countryside.
ex2: Uncle tends to ramble at weddings, and his toast to the couple lasted twenty minutes.

mean: say someone's idea again in your own words
ex: Students must paraphrase the textbook in their projects, not paste whole paragraphs from it.
note: 'To paraphrase Gandhi...' means you give his idea, not his exact words.
ex2: Let me paraphrase what the electrician said: the wiring is old and the whole flat needs new fuses.

mean: suggest something unpleasant about someone in an indirect way
ex: Mrs Kapoor never said it outright, but she managed to insinuate that the new cook was stealing sugar.
note: Stronger than imply: insinuate always suggests something bad, in a sly way.
ex2: In cross-examination, lawyers sometimes insinuate that a witness is lying without ever saying so directly.

mean: using more words than needed
ex: The verbose circular from head office took three pages to say that Friday was a holiday.
note: The opposite of concise. Teachers often write it beside padded exam answers.
ex2: My verbose uncle cannot simply say yes; every answer comes with a story from 1985.

mean: special words used by one group that outsiders find hard to follow
ex: The bank manager's jargon about 'floating rates' and 'tenure' left my parents completely confused.
note: Jargon is uncountable: say 'a lot of jargon', never 'jargons'.
ex2: Cricket commentators use jargon like 'silly point' and 'doosra' that baffles first-time viewers.

mean: a dull remark said so often that it means very little
ex: After the results, Sonia was tired of hearing the platitude that 'marks don't decide your future'.
note: A cliché is any overused phrase; a platitude is overused advice or comfort.
ex2: Instead of a real plan for the flooded roads, the official offered the platitude that 'things will improve'.

mean: deliberate exaggeration, used for effect
ex: Saying the Bengaluru traffic made him 'age ten years' was hyperbole, but only slightly.
note: Say hye-PUR-buh-lee, four syllables, not 'hyper-bowl'.
ex2: Film trailers are full of hyperbole, calling every movie 'the biggest blockbuster of the decade'.
